result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.union()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the union of this graph with another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L12218-L12296){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.union(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Set algebra on graphs](/assets/graphs/algo-set-algebra.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three panels illustrating the union of two graphs on the same four nodes. On the left, G1 has three edges, two of which (drawn in the accent color) are unique to it. In the middle, G2 has three edges, two of which (drawn in teal) are unique to it, plus one shared edge in default ink. On the right, the union graph carries every edge from either source: the two accent edges from G1, the two teal edges from G2, and the shared ink edge." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing all nodes and edges from both graphs. Nodes with the same ID are merged (this graph's attributes take precedence). Duplicate edges are not added. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to union with. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph containing all nodes and edges from both graphs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness (one directed, one undirected). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Union takes the pointwise superset of nodes and edges, merging any nodes that share an ID; where attributes clash, the calling graph wins. Both operands must agree on directedness, because there is no principled way to fold a directed edge into an undirected graph without losing information. If either operand is weighted, so is the result. Use `disjoint_union()` when you want to keep node IDs strictly separate. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes and edges from both graphs are combined -- "B" appears in both, so it's merged rather than duplicated: ::: {#4bde8462 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g1.add_node(label="A") g1.add_node(label="B") g1.add_edge("A", "B") g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g2.add_node(label="B") g2.add_node(label="C") g2.add_edge("B", "C") result = g1.union(g2) result.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#157afe90 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: This makes union a natural way to combine two snapshots of the same network taken at different times, folding in whatever new nodes or edges appeared: ::: {#4e9145f0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} t1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) t1.add_path_graph(3) # 1-2-3 t2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): t2.add_node() t2.add_edge(1, 3) # a new direct connection combined = t1.union(t2) combined.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
